newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Royalist stronghold may fall to Hun Sen troops.
newsitem.headline: Royalist stronghold may fall to Hun Sen troops.

text.p: Despite an air of calm on Tuesday, this stronghold of troops and supporters loyal to ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh could be overrun by advancing forces of strongman Hun Sen, opposition sources said.

This town on the western border with Thailand was quiet due to an informal ceasefire between royalist forces and those of Hun Sen. But officers loyal to Ranariddh said tension was mounting and morale was waning.

Poipet is still under the control of about 300 royalist troops. The danger seemed remote as people played volleyball near the roadside, others packed into home video theatres and traders crossed over into Thailand to do business.

"We've had a ceasefire agreement since last week when troops from both sides were ordered to stand still," Niek Siri, a liaison officer for Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, told Reuters from his home where mounds of weapons were piled against the wall.
Hun Sen's forces took control of Phnom Penh after a bloody grab for power on July 5-6 in the capital. Some fighting continued in other parts of the country, including the northwest.

Niek Siri, who is also the town administrator, said troops in this part of northwestern Cambodia were now quiet as they waited for political negotiations in Phnom Penh, but said they did not expect a quick solution.
"In my opinion I think it would take at least one month to make the political solution," Siri said.
In a three-hour visit, the only gunshot heard was when a royalist soldier shot a fish in a small stream.
But FUNCINPEC officers said the calm would not last long.
"We have urged the Thai authorities to help evacuate us from here," said a major of the FUNCINPEC troops, adding the soldiers feared advancing Hun Sen troops.
"For the time being we are safe here but Hun Sen's troops are creeping in slowly and sooner or later the fighting will break out and I don't think we can hold it," another royalist officer said.
Several hundred FUNCINPEC and other opposition politicians and party supporters who fear reprisals from Hun Sen troops were also holed up in Poipet, adding to the tension.
"At least these people should be evacuated from here before the fighting breaks out," the officer said.

At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded in the July 5-6 fighting in Phnom Penh. Western official said at least 25 people captured in the fighting and its aftermath, including several senior FUNCINPEC officials, had been killed.
A former Khmer Rouge commander who defected to the government said Hun Sen could easily control this region.

"If Hun Sen wanted to use force to overrun these areas he can make it easily, but maybe they can find a political solution on this issue," Sok Pheap, commander of the Democratic National United Movement (DNUM) told Reuters on the border.
Sok Pheap, who commands hundreds of DNUM troops based about five kms (three miles) south of Poipet, said his movement would keep neutral in the current conflict.

DNUM was founded last August when thousands of Khmer Rouge broke away from hardline leader Pol Pot. The Khmer Rouge were responsible for the deaths of more than one million Cambodians during their 1975-79 reign of terror.
